name: Mast cell
markers: FcεRI (the high-affinity IgE receptor; basophils carry it too)
Tryptase and chymase (granule proteases; human skin mast cells make both)
CD203c (human marker; basophils carry it too)
CD63 (reaches the surface when granules are released)
MRGPRX2 (human marker; mice use the related Mrgprb2)
summary: A tissue cell packed with granules of histamine, proteases and TNF, found beside blood vessels, nerves and body surfaces such as skin. Allergen cross-linking its IgE-coated receptors, or injury or microbes, makes it empty its granules within minutes: vessels leak and neutrophils and eosinophils are called in. It is central to allergic reactions.
functions: Does not mature in the blood. Progenitors made in the bone marrow circulate in small numbers and finish developing in tissues under stem cell factor, the ligand of KIT; human CD34-positive, KIT-positive progenitors give rise to mast cells in culture. In mice, fate-mapping shows that most adult mast cells in skin and other connective tissues come from embryonic precursors and keep themselves going in place, while bone marrow stem cells supply more of the mucosal ones. The balance in people is less clear.

Releases its granules within minutes when allergen or parasite antigen cross-links IgE bound to its FcεRI receptors (degranulation). The granules hold histamine, heparin, the proteases tryptase and chymase, and ready-made TNF. Histamine widens small vessels and makes them leaky, causing the redness and swelling of an allergic reaction in skin.

Makes new mediators after degranulation: lipids such as prostaglandin D2 and leukotriene C4 within minutes, then cytokines and chemokines over hours. Prostaglandin D2 helps draw in eosinophils and basophils.

Can also be switched on without IgE: by complement fragments C3a and C5a, by Toll-like receptor ligands, by alarmins such as IL-33 through ST2, and by neuropeptides and some drugs through MRGPRX2 (Mrgprb2 in mice). This causes allergic-type 'pseudo-allergic' reactions with no IgE involved.

Gives an early alarm in bacterial infection: its ready-made TNF is one of the first signals that bring neutrophils in. In mouse peritonitis models, mice without mast cells died more often, and the protection came back when mast cells were restored.
Breaks down some toxins with its proteases. In mice, mast cell proteases degraded components of snake and honeybee venoms and limited the toxicity of endothelin-1.
Expands at mucosal surfaces during worm infection, helped by T-cell cytokines such as IL-3 and IL-9, and releases proteases that speed worm expulsion (mouse evidence).

Shapes the cells around it. In mouse skin, mast cell TNF helped dendritic cells leave for the lymph node early in a contact allergy test, and human mast cells and basophils expressing CD40L plus IL-4 can switch B cells to making IgE in culture.

Is held in check by neighbours. Regulatory T cells touch mast cells through OX40 on the T cell and OX40L on the mast cell, which blocks degranulation (shown in mouse cells). In mouse dermis, group 2 innate lymphoid cells sit beside mast cells and make IL-13, which suppresses them.

Comes in tissue-specific types: human skin and connective tissue mast cells carry both tryptase and chymase, while mucosal ones carry mainly tryptase. Mouse connective tissue and mucosal types differ in a similar but not identical way.

Debated: how widely mast cells matter outside IgE-driven allergy. Many proposed roles (in bacterial defence, wound healing and more) came from mice with mutations in Kit, which also lack other cell types. Newer mouse models that remove mast cells more selectively have confirmed some of these roles but not reproduced others.
abundance: Not found in healthy blood. Found in almost every tissue, most densely near the body's surfaces (skin, airways, gut) and around blood vessels, nerves and lymph vessels. Counts differ by tissue and body site and rise in allergy and some parasite infections.
